article_title: Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students’ Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety
citation: Amanda J. Rockinson-Szapkiw, Jillian Wendt, and Rebecca Lunde. (2013). Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety. American Journal of Distance Education, 27(3), 179-188. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923647.2013.796230
title: Adopt e-textbooks in collegiate classrooms to support students' self-regulated learning strategy use
description: The article recommends offering e-textbooks in collegiate courses because its findings indicate e-textbook users were more likely to employ self-regulated learning strategies while reading. E-textbooks provide "flexible, interactive, manipulative, constructive, active, and searchable elements" that let students make notes, highlight, and explore material nonlinearly. The recommendation rests on a self-selection study with small effect sizes.
requirements: Courses must offer the primary textbook in both e-textbook and print format so students can choose, as the studied bookstore did
constraints: The article reports the effect sizes for the strategy differences were low, indicating little practical significance
Students self-selected format rather than being randomly assigned
Prior studies of e-textbook influence on learning and motivation reported mixed results
target_learners: university undergraduate, masters, and doctoral students in online and face-to-face education courses
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use while reading course textbooks
examples: In the study, 59 face-to-face and online courses offered the primary textbook in both formats during spring 2012, and 106 students chose e-textbooks while 432 chose print
key_sources: Amanda J. Rockinson-Szapkiw, Jillian Wendt, and Rebecca Lunde. (2013). Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety. American Journal of Distance Education, 27(3), 179-188. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923647.2013.796230

article_title: Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited
citation: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0
title: E-Tutor: a web-delivered ILTS for German with modular NLP answer processing, adaptive learner modeling, and curriculum-aligned activities
description: E-Tutor (renamed from German Tutor in 2003, expanded 2009) is an Intelligent Language Tutoring System for learners of German as a foreign language, used in regular university classroom instruction. It uses a modular answer-processing architecture in which "if any error checking module detects an error, further processing is blocked", so only one error at a time is displayed. It implements "10 different activity types for each of the 15 chapters", covering vocabulary, grammar, listening/reading comprehension, culture, pronunciation and writing, and follows the sequence of the textbook Deutsch: Na klar!
requirements: Must process and analyze learner input with a linguistically sophisticated system equipped with a grammar and parser that detects grammatical errors
Must keep a record of student work and performance shareable with instructors and follow the course book's grammatical and vocabulary sequence
constraints: The initial system was limited to content commonly taught in the first semester of university language instruction
Client-end Java applets caused compatibility issues, leading to a rewrite in plain-vanilla HTML 4.0 with frames and Javascript
target_learners: University learners of German as a foreign language at beginner and intermediate proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: German grammar (e.g., subject-verb agreement, article usage, relative clauses, passive constructions)
vocabulary, pronunciation, listening and reading comprehension, cultural knowledge, and writing skills
examples: The 2003 upgrade rewrote the Prolog grammar in Java with JSP pages and servlets, yielding a significant (10:1) improvement in system responsiveness and load handling
A context-sensitive help function links grammatical errors to runtime-constructed inflectional paradigms geared at the specific learner mistake
key_sources: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0

article_title: Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited
citation: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0
title: E-Tutor's dynamic learner model: skill-specific scores and phrase descriptors modulate feedback and remediation
description: E-Tutor's learner model provides a dynamic assessment of each learner by considering past and current performance and behavior. The grammar and parser generate phrase descriptors, frame structures modeling grammatical phenomena (e.g., subject-verb agreement, noun gender) with values correct, error, or absent, which "correspond to structures in the learner model and are the interface medium between the learner model and the grammar". For each grammar constraint the model keeps a per-student score that increases or decreases with evidence of successful or unsuccessful use; feedback wording and amount depend on the learner's rank (novice vs. expert) per skill, and remedial exercises target individual weaknesses.
requirements: A fully specified lexicon and a grammar and parser that generate phrase descriptors for each grammatical constraint
Separation of feedback generation from linguistic analysis and learning activity so feedback messages can be adjusted per exercise
constraints: Scores for each grammar skill are tracked independently, so a student may be expert at one skill and novice at another
target_learners: University learners of German as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: Individualized error-contingent feedback and remediation across German grammar skills
examples: The system might change the order in which errors are displayed depending on the learner's past performance or the focus of the learning activity
Session summaries group mistakes into categories such as Article Inflection and Verb Inflection set by a parameter file
key_sources: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0

article_title: Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited
citation: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0
title: E-Tutor learner corpus with comparative error profiles and exercise-specific preemptive hints
description: In 2009 the authors created a learner corpus of "several million responses submitted by roughly 5000 previous learners who had completed the activity types of E-Tutor between 2003 and 2008". An interface lets learners examine interlanguage and task-specific phenomena and compare their error patterns to thousands of previous users of the same exercises. Statistical analysis of the corpus produced ranked error lists per exercise, activity type and chapter, from which the system generates exercise-specific preemptive hints displayed when students start an exercise; the number of hints can be adjusted based on prior learner performance.
requirements: The linguistic analysis of user input and the system log constructed from all user inputs, accumulated over years of classroom use
constraints: The hint ranking is based on prior student performance during 2003–2008 only
target_learners: University learners of German as a foreign language using E-Tutor in classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: Exploratory data-driven learning about interlanguage phenomena and one's own error patterns in German
examples: Fig. 5 shows comparative performance reports where a student performed much better on word order than the 4378 previous users while making more grammar and less spelling mistakes
Research (e.g., Ellis et al. 2001) is cited that preemptive feedback may lead to more successful task completion and reduce frustration
key_sources: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0

article_title: Weaving STEAM with threads: teacher professional development with e-textile projects
citation: Mustafa Sat, Kursat Cagiltay. (2026). Weaving STEAM with threads: teacher professional development with e-textile projects. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10597-z
title: Five-day e-textile-supported STEAM teacher PD camp with seven structured projects and one open-ended project
description: A five-day professional development program at a Turkish university, run as two camps for middle school science teachers, focused on "designing and developing STEAM projects using e-textile technology, with an emphasis on integrating art, design, and technology." It encompassed "seven structured e-textile projects" (badges, wristbands, necklaces, color-changing star clusters, light-sensing lighthouses, heat-sensing thermometers, color-sensing scarves) plus one open-ended project, progressing from serial and parallel circuits to sensors and Arduino programming, with hands-on projects integrating problem-based scenarios and engineering design stages adapted from Hynes et al. (2011). Five facilitators supported groups of two or three teachers.
requirements: Purposively selected teachers with little or no prior hands-on e-textile STEAM experience
Supply of e-textile materials, tools, and facilitator support throughout the program
constraints: Evaluated with self-report post-surveys and a small, voluntary follow-up sample (5 completed surveys)
target_learners: in-service middle school science teachers from rural and socioeconomically disadvantaged public schools
target_learning_goals: electricity and circuitry concepts
STEAM project design
Arduino programming basics
interdisciplinary integration of art, design, and technology
examples: Teachers designed wearable projects such as bracelets, necklaces, badges, and color-changing scarves, later implemented at a school science fair by a participant
key_sources: Mustafa Sat, Kursat Cagiltay. (2026). Weaving STEAM with threads: teacher professional development with e-textile projects. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10597-z

article_title: Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project
citation: Wrzesien, M., & Alcañiz Raya, M. (2010). Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project. In Computers & Education (Vol. 55, Issue 1, pp. 178–187). Elsevier BV. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.01.003
title: E-Junior: a serious virtual world for teaching children natural science and ecology about the Mediterranean Sea
description: E-Junior is a serious virtual world (SVW) designed "according to pedagogical theories and curricular objectives to help children learn about the Mediterranean Sea and its environmental issues while playing." It targets elementary education and combines a gaming aspect with curricular content. In its evaluation, a class taught in the SVW was compared with a traditional class with identical learning objectives and contents.
requirements: Designed according to pedagogical theories and aligned with curricular objectives
target_learners: Elementary education children
target_learning_goals: Natural science and ecology knowledge about the Mediterranean Sea and its environmental issues
examples: Evaluated with 48 children by comparing a virtual group taught in the SVW with a traditional group covering identical content without a gaming aspect
key_sources: Wrzesien, M., & Alcañiz Raya, M. (2010). Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project. In Computers & Education (Vol. 55, Issue 1, pp. 178–187). Elsevier BV. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.01.003

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education
citation: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: E-learning as ICT-enabled teaching and learning that changes teacher and learner roles and fosters learner autonomy
description: The article frames e-learning as the use and application of information and communication technologies — websites, PCs, tablet PCs, cell phones, learning management systems, TVs and radios — to improve teaching and learning processes. It defines e-learning as "a network-enabled expression associated with functions that facilitate teaching and learning in an efficient manner" (citing Cooke). It holds that ICT features "change the role of the teacher and th e learner, facilitate learning, and lead to interactive learni ng, learner autonomy, self-sufficiency, and self-co nfidence", shifting teachers from mere sources of material to supervisors of the learning process.
requirements: ICT infrastructure of adequate quality, since the article states the success of e-learning depends on the quality of ICT
constraints: The article notes e-learning and online learning are regarded to have different meanings, and terminology varies
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement, learner autonomy, self-sufficiency and self-confidence
examples: E-learning programs include web-based learning, computer-based learning, virtual classrooms and electronic activity, with content delivered via web, intranet or extranet, audio or video MP3s, satellite televisions and CD-ROMs.
key_sources: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082408

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the E-Learning Influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary Study of Virtual to Actualization
citation: Daryanto, E., Siregar, B., & Januariyansah, S. (2022). A meta-analysis of the e-learning influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary study of virtual to actualization. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science, and Technology (IJEMST), 10(3), 710-721. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijemst.2509
title: Use e-learning in VET as a complement to practical learning rather than a replacement for conventional machine-tool practice
description: Because the meta-analysis found e-learning cannot accommodate conventional practical learning using machine tools, the article recommends combining e-learning to support practical VET learning. The authors state e-learning "can be combined to support practical VET learning, which is expected to be effective due to the complementary combination". This positions e-learning as enrichment and support for hands-on learning rather than the primary form of instruction in conventional practical subjects.
requirements: Practical learning must retain real media such as machine tools; e-learning components should target theoretical content and computer-media practical work
constraints: Applies to conventional practical learning such as welding and painting; e-learning can be primary only for computer- and internet-media practical learning such as digital simulation and web programming
target_learners: Vocational high school and college VET students
target_learning_goals: Practical and performance skills in vocational trades
Theoretical understanding of vocational subjects
examples: The meta-analysis of 18 Indonesian VET studies found e-learning effective for theoretical learning and computer-media practical learning, while conventional machine-tool practice was not accommodated by e-learning
key_sources: Daryanto, E., Siregar, B., & Januariyansah, S. (2022). A meta-analysis of the e-learning influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary study of virtual to actualization. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science, and Technology (IJEMST), 10(3), 710-721. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijemst.2509

article_title: Effectiveness of E-Content Package on Teaching IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Chemistry at Undergraduate Level
citation: G. Devendiran, M. Vakkil. (2017). Effectiveness of e-content package on teaching IUPAC nomenclature of organic chemistry at undergraduate level. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 14(3), 49-54. https://journals.i-manager.com
title: E-content package on nomenclature of organic compounds
description: A self-instructional e-content package developed by the investigator to teach IUPAC nomenclature of organic compounds to undergraduate chemistry majors. It was "based upon the chapter 'Nomenclature of organic compounds'" from standard organic chemistry textbooks, and "The total duration of the e-content package was thirty seven minutes." It served as the treatment for the experimental group in the quasi-experiment and incorporated technological features such as images, audio, and video.
requirements: Requires computer and networking infrastructure through which content is presented to students in a digital environment
constraints: Developed for a specific Periyar University syllabus chapter on nomenclature of organic compounds at undergraduate level
target_learners: Undergraduate students majoring in chemistry
target_learning_goals: Applying IUPAC rules for naming organic compounds
examples: Used as the treatment in a Pre-test-Post-test Non Equivalent Groups Design with 36 experimental and 35 control students
key_sources: G. Devendiran, M. Vakkil. (2017). Effectiveness of e-content package on teaching IUPAC nomenclature of organic chemistry at undergraduate level. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 14(3), 49-54. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1171298

article_title: The Effectiveness of Electronic Mind Maps in Developing Academic Achievement and the Attitude towards Learning English among Primary School Students
citation: Afaf M. Aljaser. (2017). The Effectiveness of Electronic Mind Maps in Developing Academic Achievement and the Attitude towards Learning English among Primary School Students. International Education Studies, Vol. 10, No. 12. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p80
title: E-Mind Maps instructional unit for fifth-grade English (I Mind Maps software with a reviewed teacher guide)
description: An instructional treatment in which the study unit was taught using electronic Mind Maps created with I Mind Maps software, which the article says can "create relations among information, connect old and new knowledge, and correct errors without duplication". The author prepared a teacher guide covering the unit's objectives, an overview of the e-Mind Maps strategy, a time plan, and educational tools, which was reviewed by specialists in curriculum and English instruction before use. The unit was taught to the experimental group in 5 classes of 45 minutes each over 5 weeks, while the control group received the traditional teacher-guide method.
requirements: A teacher guide prepared and reviewed by specialized reviewers to judge objectives, teaching plans, and lesson formatting according to e-Mind Maps
Computer software containing drawings, cliparts, symbols, and images that can be easily inserted
constraints: Tested only with fifth-grade female students at one private school in Riyadh, ages 10 to 12
target_learners: fifth-grade primary female students
target_learning_goals: English language achievement (grammatical rules and vocabulary of the study unit)
positive attitudes towards learning English
examples: The proposed study unit was taught to the experimental group using e-Mind Maps and to the control group by the traditional method, with pre- and post-tests administered in February and March 2017
key_sources: Afaf M. Aljaser. (2017). The Effectiveness of Electronic Mind Maps in Developing Academic Achievement and the Attitude towards Learning English among Primary School Students. International Education Studies, Vol. 10, No. 12. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p80

article_title: Repeated E-Book Reading and Its Contribution to Learning New Words among Kindergartners
citation: Ofra Korat, Olla Kozlov-Peretz, Ora Segal-Drori. (2017). Repeated E-book Reading and Its Contribution to Learning New Words among Kindergartners. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 7. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i7.2498
title: E-book with built-in dictionary mode (Confused Yuval) for independent kindergarten reading
description: An electronic version of the Hebrew storybook Yuval Hamebulbal (Confused Yuval) by Miriam Roth, used in its "Read story with dictionary" mode. The mode "offers an oral reading of the text together with explanations of difficult words (10 words) that appear automatically on the screen after the entire page has been read by the narrator", and children can reactivate these words. Each difficult word is enunciated clearly and associated with pictures supporting its meaning, allowing children to read independently without adult help.
requirements: Children can activate dictionary hotspots themselves; the study asked each child to press on the dictionary word so the meaning was provided again, twice per session
constraints: Not all difficult words in the story received a dictionary explanation (10 of 18 assessed words were explained)
target_learners: Kindergartners aged 5-6 from low socioeconomic status backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Receptive vocabulary
Word explanation
Word production in story retelling
examples: In the study, each child completed two individual reading sessions; in each session the child heard the meaning of each dictionary word three times, for a total of six exposures
key_sources: Ofra Korat, Olla Kozlov-Peretz, Ora Segal-Drori. (2017). Repeated E-book Reading and Its Contribution to Learning New Words among Kindergartners. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 7. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i7.2498

article_title: A Cluster Randomized Pilot Trial of the Equity-Explicit Establish-Maintain-Restore Program among High School Teachers and Students
citation: Mylien T. Duong, Larissa M. Gaias, Eric Brown, Sharon Kiche, Lillian Nguyen, Catherine M. Corbin, Cassandra J. Chandler, Joanne J. Buntain-Ricklefs, Clayton R. Cook. (2022). A Cluster Randomized Pilot Trial of the Equity-Explicit Establish-Maintain-Restore Program among High School Teachers and Students. School Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12310-022-09516-3
title: Equity-Explicit Establish-Maintain-Restore (E-EMR): a three-phase teacher relationship framework with interwoven equity levers
description: E-EMR is a professional-development framework for student–teacher relationships organized around three sequential-but-flexible phases: Establish, Maintain, and Restore. The article states "EMR is a framework that provides shared language and concrete practices to promote STR", with eight establish practices, a 5-to-1 positive-to-negative interaction ratio for Maintain, and four Restore strategies. Four equity levers (Seek Commonalities, Gain Perspective, Gather Facts to Disprove Assumptions, Know your Vulnerabilities) were added to interrupt implicit bias, and the equity content was interwoven throughout each practice rather than siloed.
requirements: Teachers receive initial training plus ongoing implementation supports (PLC protocols, playbook, weekly emails) to enact the phases and equity levers
A triage process focuses teacher attention on students who need relationship support most, since practices cannot feasibly be distributed equally across all students at the high school level
constraints: The dyadic nature of most practices makes them difficult for high school teachers to implement with all their students given limited time across many class periods
E-EMR was developed and previously tested as an in-person intervention, making fidelity difficult to measure in distance settings
target_learners: Ninth-grade high school students
Racially minoritized students
target_learning_goals: Student–teacher relationship quality
School belonging
Academic motivation and engagement
examples: In the pilot trial, teachers in three schools received a six-hour interactive training with an elicit-provide-elicit structure, monthly structured PLCs, and weekly email prompts with an equity tip
key_sources: Mylien T. Duong, Larissa M. Gaias, Eric Brown, Sharon Kiche, Lillian Nguyen, Catherine M. Corbin, Cassandra J. Chandler, Joanne J. Buntain-Ricklefs, Clayton R. Cook. (2022). A Cluster Randomized Pilot Trial of the Equity-Explicit Establish-Maintain-Restore Program among High School Teachers and Students. School Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12310-022-09516-3

article_title: A Cluster Randomized Pilot Trial of the Equity-Explicit Establish-Maintain-Restore Program among High School Teachers and Students
citation: Mylien T. Duong, Larissa M. Gaias, Eric Brown, Sharon Kiche, Lillian Nguyen, Catherine M. Corbin, Cassandra J. Chandler, Joanne J. Buntain-Ricklefs, Clayton R. Cook. (2022). A Cluster Randomized Pilot Trial of the Equity-Explicit Establish-Maintain-Restore Program among High School Teachers and Students. School Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12310-022-09516-3
title: E-EMR implementation support package: training, playbook, PLC protocols, and weekly equity-tip emails
description: Beyond the core relationship practices, E-EMR includes a set of implementation supports the article describes as "training, a 'playbook' with implementation scripts, structured professional learning community (PLC) protocols, and weekly email prompts". The six-hour initial training covered STR rationale, implicit-bias science, and equitable implementation, and was coded for fidelity (97–100% adherence; 96% behavioral engagement). The monthly PLC protocol guides teachers through six steps including reviewing progress, identifying students in Establish or Restore phases, reflecting on equity by examining how student demographics relate to relationship phase, and setting student-specific goals.
requirements: Monthly small-group PLC meetings following the six-step structured protocol
Weekly email prompts including an equity tip tied to the experiences of students of color
constraints: Fidelity of the intervention could not be measured when COVID-19 moved schooling to distance settings, so T3 data were excluded from the study
target_learners: Ninth-grade high school teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher implementation of equity-explicit relationship-building practices
Disrupting teacher implicit bias
examples: Trainings were videotaped and coded for fidelity, with trainers delivering 97–100% of active components and teacher behavioral engagement at 96% of observed intervals
key_sources: Mylien T. Duong, Larissa M. Gaias, Eric Brown, Sharon Kiche, Lillian Nguyen, Catherine M. Corbin, Cassandra J. Chandler, Joanne J. Buntain-Ricklefs, Clayton R. Cook. (2022). A Cluster Randomized Pilot Trial of the Equity-Explicit Establish-Maintain-Restore Program among High School Teachers and Students. School Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12310-022-09516-3

article_title: E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization
citation: Yachina, N. P., Valeeva, L. A., & Sirazeeva, A. F. (2016). E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-442.
title: Six requirements for designing e-teaching materials for humanities disciplines in future teachers' training
description: The article identifies and rationalizes a set of design requirements for e-teaching materials for humanities disciplines in future teachers' training. As stated, the article "identifies and rationalizes the requirements (integrative framework, gradual development of materials, marked structure, individualization of the teaching process, the strategic character of knowledge assimilation, openness of the system) for the design of e -teaching materials for the humanities disciplines in th e training of future teachers." The requirements respond to the finding that existing e-resources' structure and content "do not always meet the didactic requirements."
requirements: Design must follow the six named requirements: integrative framework, gradual development of materials, marked structure, individualization of the teaching process, strategic character of knowledge assimilation, and openness of the system.
constraints: The requirements were developed for humanities disciplines in the training of future teachers.
target_learners: future humanities teachers at university
target_learning_goals: design and use of e-teaching materials integrating subject and methodological training
examples: The developed e-teaching materials for the 'Teaching proficiency' course were built to these requirements and pilot-tested at the university.
key_sources: Yachina, N. P., Valeeva, L. A., & Sirazeeva, A. F. (2016). E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-442. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094652

article_title: E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization
citation: Yachina, N. P., Valeeva, L. A., & Sirazeeva, A. F. (2016). E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-442.
title: E-teaching materials for the 'Teaching proficiency' course with subject-oriented and methodological modules
description: The developed artifact is a set of e-teaching materials for the 'Teaching proficiency' course, used in training future History and English language teachers. It "include[s] the following modules:1) subject ori ented (containing an e -textbook, consisting of theoretical, practical and control and diagnostics modules); 2) methodological (includes course steering document, methodological recommendations on e-teaching materials use, interactive assignments and manuals on e -teaching materials use)." Content is supported by text, audio, video, graphics and animation. In the experiment, tests for experimental groups were offered "in electronic form as one of the modules of e -teaching materials."
requirements: Content must be supported by text, audio, video, graphics, animation, determined according to didactics.
constraints: Designed for humanities disciplines in future teachers' training at Kazan (Volga region) Federal University.
target_learners: full-time and part-time university students of History and the English language faculty
target_learning_goals: subject knowledge and skills in the 'Teaching proficiency' course
methodological skills of using e-teaching materials in the learning process
examples: The materials were pilot tested in the formative experiment (2012-2013) against traditional teaching forms with 54 participants.
key_sources: Yachina, N. P., Valeeva, L. A., & Sirazeeva, A. F. (2016). E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-442. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094652

article_title: Effectiveness of E-TLM in Learning Vocabulary in English
citation: Singaravelu, G. (2011). Effectiveness of e-TLM in Learning Vocabulary in English. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 1 No. 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ976543
title: Multimedia e-TLM package for English vocabulary at standard VI
description: An electronic teaching-learning material package prepared by the researcher to teach English vocabulary to standard VI pupils, used in the classroom for one week. The study reports that "Electronic TLM is capturing the attention of the learners immediately" and that it "ensures the gaining motivation of the learners". It served as the independent variable in the parallel-group experiment.
requirements: Classroom execution of activities through the e-TLM package, as in the study's five-step procedure
constraints: The study is confined to 60 students of standard VI in one school and to vocabulary of the state board text book only
target_learners: standard VI (upper-primary) pupils
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary acquisition
examples: Used for one week of classroom vocabulary instruction with standard VI pupils in Coimbatore

article_title: Pedagogical impact of different levels of e-learning teaching during anesthesia residency: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: Jean S, Thill J, Burey J, Besnier E, Lambert M, Lefevre-Scelles A, Abily J, Gastaldi G, Allard E, Hanouz J-L, Veber B, Dureuil B, Thill C, Compère V. (2026). Pedagogical impact of different levels of e-learning teaching during anesthesia residency: a randomized clinical trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09225-4
title: Four-level stratification of e-learning: passive, guided, interactive, adaptive
description: The article organizes e-learning in medical education into four levels: "passive, guided, interactive, and adaptive". Passive e-learning offers static content with limited engagement; guided e-learning provides structured pathways with interactive elements; interactive e-learning "actively involves learners in simulations and decision-making"; and adaptive e-learning personalizes content to individual needs. The article uses this stratification to explain heterogeneous results across e-learning studies and to position its intervention as interactive (Level 3) e-learning.
requirements: The choice among levels depends on the educational objectives and available resources, as the article states
constraints: Adaptive e-learning is described as technologically complex and costly; interactive e-learning requires more resources than passive
target_learners: anesthesia residents
medical trainees

clinical reasoning

article_title: Faculty perceptions and use of e-learning resources for medical education and future predictions.
citation: Kim Kyong-Jee, Kim Giwoon, Kang Youngjoon. (2023). Faculty perceptions and use of e-learning resources for medical education and future predictions. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2023.270
title: e-MedEdu: the Korean medical schools' consortium e-learning portal and resource repository
description: e-MedEdu (www.mededu.or.kr) is "the e-learning portal of the consortium of Korean medical schools", which "offers a repository of over 1,700 online resources in basic and clinical medicines", contributed to by approximately 250 medical teachers since 2008, with an average annual website hit of over 200,000. Its resources include "clinical cases, images, videos, sounds, online modules, and multimedia assessment items." The study surveyed full-time faculty registered as users of this portal.
requirements: Contributions from medical teachers since 2008 sustain the repository
constraints: The study found faculty wanted the repository expanded and contents mapped with national standards for learning outcomes
target_learners: Medical faculty members
Medical students in Korean medical schools
target_learning_goals: Access to shared e-learning resources in basic and clinical medicine
examples: About two-thirds of survey respondents had used the portal for 1-10 years
Clinical videos were reported as the most popular contents in e-MedEdu

article_title: [Interactive electronic visualization formats in student teaching].
citation: van Bonn Sara M., Grajek Jan S., Rettschlag Stefanie, Schraven Sebastian P., Mlynski Robert. (2024). Interactive electronic visualization formats in student teaching. Hno. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-024-01436-9
title: Electronic ward round (E-Visite): live-streamed bedside teaching via tablet and Zoom
description: The electronic ward round replaced the suspended in-person ENT clerkship once weekly: a mentor streamed real-time bedside teaching via the Zoom app on a 9th-generation iPad, with patient presentations, demonstrations of examination techniques, and microscope/endoscope camera findings shown on screen. Groups of 7–10 students joined with a weekly changing password, and the roughly 60-minute session allowed questions and chat interaction. The article states "Der digitale Unterricht am Krankenbett erfolgte einmal wöchentlich für jeweils eine Gruppe zu einem vorher festgelegten Termin."
requirements: Patients gave written consent for anonymized transmission of history and disease presentations for training purposes
The platform must use secure encryption technology to ensure confidentiality of patient data, per the discussion
constraints: Practical skills such as examination techniques and patient contact could only be conveyed at a theoretical level
target_learners: Seventh-semester medical students in the ENT block clerkship
target_learning_goals: Learning history-taking and fundamentals of clinical findings
Becoming familiar with ENT disease presentations
examples: Clinical findings were captured with a camera on the ear microscope or endoscopes and shown to students on a screen

article_title: An e-Problem-Based Learning Program for Infection Control in Nursing Homes: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Choi Young-Rim, Lee Ye-Na, Kim Dayeong, Park Won Hee, Kwon Dai Young, Chang Sung Ok. (2022). An e-Problem-Based Learning Program for Infection Control in Nursing Homes: A Quasi-Experimental Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192013371
title: e-PBL-based infection control education program for nursing home staff (three chapters, web-based, chatbot-supported)
description: A web-based problem-based learning program for South Korean nursing home staff, built on infection control cases from staff interviews and structured as "three chapters" covering common infections, signs and symptoms, and identifying/assessing infection, plus a review chapter. Activities include video viewing, individual and group assignments, discussion with other learners, and self- and peer review. Learner–learner and teacher–learner interactions are supported via instant messaging and a chatbot, and the program was available online for two weeks.
requirements: Learners able to use computers (individuals with computer difficulties were excluded)
Staff availability for a 2–3 hour web-based training period
constraints: The article states the program will need adaptation to a mobile device environment to enhance accessibility
Satisfaction was 3.5 out of 5, described as leaving room for improvement
target_learners: Nurses, care workers, and nursing assistants in nursing homes
target_learning_goals: Early detection and prevention of infection in nursing home residents
Critical thinking disposition for infection control
examples: Delivered via website for two weeks beginning 30 December 2021, with guided orientation meetings and research-team chatbot support

article_title: Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform.
citation: Kremser Wolfgang, Kranzinger Stefan, Bernhart Severin. (2021). Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s21238042
title: e-GAL: a five-module system design for e-learning platforms supporting gesture-aided learning
description: e-GAL is a system design for e-learning platforms with gesture-aided learning (GAL) support, built around decoupling learning content from gestures so recorded gestures can be shared and reused. It comprises five modules: a content catalog, a gesture catalog, a lesson configurator for instructors, a web-based lesson player with an animated humanoid avatar, and a monitoring module that records learner motion data for instructor review. The article states: "This section proposes the e-GAL design, a system design for e-learning platforms with GAL support." A lesson is an ordered list of gesture-enhanced content items (GECs).
requirements: Gesture data must be sufficient to animate a humanoid avatar; ideally recorded with a high-quality motion-capture system
The monitoring module requires a motion sensor (e.g., accelerometer, video) chosen according to the gesture's range of motion
constraints: The design is open regarding the type of learning content but was developed specifically for this study
The article states the study does not say anything about the influence of this mode of learning on learning outcomes
target_learners: Remote e-learning learners, demonstrated with adult participants learning German vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary/word learning via gesture-aided rehearsal; extendable to other learning content types
examples: A reference implementation deployed the five modules in a microservice pattern with 64 German words, XSENS motion-captured gestures, a Unity WebGL lesson player, and webcam-based monitoring
key_sources: Kremser Wolfgang, Kranzinger Stefan, Bernhart Severin. (2021). Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s21238042

article_title: Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform.
citation: Kremser Wolfgang, Kranzinger Stefan, Bernhart Severin. (2021). Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s21238042
title: e-GAL reference implementation for German word learning (Unity WebGL player, XSENS gestures, webcam monitoring)
description: A working reference implementation of the e-GAL design built to learn German words. The content catalog held 64 German words with text and WaveNet synthesized speech in PostgreSQL; gestures were recorded with the XSENS MTw Awinda full-body motion-capture system and exported as FBX files; the lesson player was a Unity 3D WebGL application featuring the robot-like avatar Y-Bot; and the webcam recorded learners during each GEC for upload to the monitoring log. The article reports: "The lesson player (Figure 5) of the reference implementation was a Unity 3D [32] application running in a WebGL environment."
requirements: Learners assumed to sit behind a desk in front of a screen so the webcam captures at least the upper body
Gestures chosen so they can be performed while sitting behind a desk
constraints: The avatar's extremities lacked collision boxes, so hands clipped into rather than touching each other
The XSENS skeletal model has only a rough positioning of the hands
target_learners: Adult remote learners (12 female, 7 male, mean age 36.6) with basic knowledge of using web applications
target_learning_goals: German vocabulary learning with gesture enactment
examples: The authors created a lesson of six GEC items with the lesson configurator; GEC order was randomized with the same seed for each participant
key_sources: Kremser Wolfgang, Kranzinger Stefan, Bernhart Severin. (2021). Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s21238042

article_title: Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform.
citation: Kremser Wolfgang, Kranzinger Stefan, Bernhart Severin. (2021). Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s21238042
title: e-GAL reference implementation as a remote gesture-data collection and annotation tool
description: Beyond its educational purpose, the article identifies a second use case for the reference implementation: collecting and labeling large amounts of gesture data remotely. During the field test the monitoring log accumulated 491 webcam-recorded gesture execution videos that instructors could review and label in the monitoring module's web interface. The article notes: "It can collect and label large amounts of gesture data remotely and with little effort." The authors suggest this can be used, for instance, to generate large gesture datasets for machine learning.
requirements: Better instructing participants and consistently checking framing before and during the lesson, since webcam framing was inconsistent and quality varied
constraints: The main issue in the video clips was inconsistent framing of the participant and varying webcam quality
target_learners: Adult remote participants contributing gesture execution recordings
target_learning_goals: Gesture data collection and annotation supporting gesture recognition research rather than direct learner outcomes
examples: The system test log contained 491 GEC execution videos that were labeled Correct, Poor, or Wrong via the monitoring module's web interface
key_sources: Kremser Wolfgang, Kranzinger Stefan, Bernhart Severin. (2021). Design and Implementation of a Gesture-Aided E-Learning Platform. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s21238042

article_title: Effectiveness of E-Learning Program in Preventing WP Smoking in Adolescent Females in West of Iran by Applying Prototype-Willingness Model: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Bashirian S, Barati M, Karami M, Hamzeh B, Ezati E. (2020). Effectiveness of E-Learning Program in Preventing WP Smoking in Adolescent Females in West of Iran by Applying Prototype-Willingness Model: A Randomized Controlled Trial. J Res Health Sci. 20(4): e00497. https://doi.org/10.34172/jrhs.2020.31
title: Five-session e-learning program with gated videos and electronic booklet for water pipe smoking prevention
description: The intervention was delivered on the e-learning management system of Hamadan University of Medical Sciences, with a personal page, username and password for each participant. It consisted of "educational materials, such as videos and an electronic training booklet" across 5 weekly sessions. Each session ended with 3 questions; participants answering incorrectly had to rewatch the tutorial clip before advancing. Post-test questionnaires were completed by self-report 3 months after the intervention.
requirements: Participants need system access training, personal credentials, and correct answers to session questions to progress to the next clips
constraints: Participants absent twice from training sessions or missing the post-test were excluded
target_learners: adolescent female middle and high school students
target_learning_goals: reducing willingness, intention, positive attitudes, norms, and prototypes toward water pipe smoking
examples: The program was based on behavioral change techniques identified in web-based interventions: providing information about consequences of unhealthy behavior and skill training to reduce willingness to engage in high-risk behavior

article_title: Evaluation of new motorized articulating laparoscopic instruments by laparoscopic novices using a standardized laparoscopic skills curriculum.
citation: Uysal Daniel, Gasch Claudia, Behnisch Rouven, Nickel Felix, Müller-Stich Beat Peter, Hohenfellner Markus, Teber Dogu. (2020). Evaluation of new motorized articulating laparoscopic instruments by laparoscopic novices using a standardized laparoscopic skills curriculum. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-020-08086-2
title: E-BLUS: European training in basic laparoscopic urological skills examination
description: E-BLUS is a validated laparoscopic skills curriculum used by the European Association of Urology to certify Urology laparoscopists. The article states it "was developed to specifically evaluate the competence of basic laparoscopic skills in Urology residents and consists of four exercises: peg transfer (PT), cutting a circle (CC), needle guidance (NG), and laparoscopic suturing (LS)". In this study it served as the standardized task set, with time tolerance adjusted for novices and time, errors, and exercise failure recorded.
requirements: An official exercise video tutorial was watched prior to each exercise
Time tolerance of the exercises was adjusted to account for participant inexperience
constraints: The article notes the E-BLUS examination was especially designed for the ergonomics of CLI and not for ALI, so using only its four basic tasks could be a limitation
target_learners: Urology residents
laparoscopic novices
target_learning_goals: basic laparoscopic skills competence
examples: Participants completed peg transfer, cutting a circle, needle guidance, and laparoscopic suturing in a box trainer with 2D vision after three warm-up tasks
key_sources: Uysal Daniel, Gasch Claudia, Behnisch Rouven, Nickel Felix, Müller-Stich Beat Peter, Hohenfellner Markus, Teber Dogu. (2020). Evaluation of new motorized articulating laparoscopic instruments by laparoscopic novices using a standardized laparoscopic skills curriculum. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-020-08086-2
